#9605. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9604. When AI Localization Translates a Promise You Cannot Keep

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero illustration. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The translated page reads beautifully. The call to action works. The search annotations pass a technical check.

The page also promises a product feature that is not available in the reader's market.

Translation quality did not prevent the failure because the failure was not linguistic. A commercial claim crossed a regional boundary without being checked against regional facts.

I would treat AI localization as a release process for a local promise, not merely a process for producing text in another language. Fluency, product accuracy, technical delivery, and search configuration need separate checks.

A language can serve several markets. A market can require several languages. Neither alone determines product eligibility, currency, commercial terms, or the correct sales destination.

Start by identifying the intended audience precisely enough for the decision. A Spanish-language educational article may serve readers across regions, while a product offer may require market-specific availability and terms.

Do not create unnecessary regional copies merely because a localization tool can generate them. Each additional version creates a maintenance obligation and another place where a promise can drift.

Conversely, do not force materially different offers into one universal translated page. If the underlying product or commercial facts differ, the content architecture needs to preserve that difference rather than hide it in a vague footnote.

The proposed design is a matrix of language, market, product scope, and intended action. It is not a claim that every company needs a separate URL for every combination. The right structure depends on the actual differences that readers need to understand.

A shared claim might explain a general workflow or product concept. A local fact might state an available payment method, support arrangement, product edition, price, tax treatment, or delivery condition.

Keep local facts in a reviewed source of record rather than asking the translation model to infer them. A model can preserve approved values or flag missing ones; it should not choose a plausible regional offer because the source page lacks detail.

For each consequential fact, record its owner, effective date, scope, and review condition. Product marketing may own feature descriptions, while finance or the relevant commercial team owns approved pricing. Legal terms require the appropriate review rather than a linguistic approximation.

Do not confuse a disclaimer with a correction. A large promise at the top of a page remains misleading if a small note below quietly withdraws it for most readers.

The local version should state the applicable promise clearly where the reader makes the decision. If the correct fact is unknown, hold the affected claim or action until it can be verified.

Imagine a software company translating a page from English into German. The source says the product includes a particular payment capability. The capability is available only in selected markets and editions.

The translator preserves the sentence accurately. The local page is therefore faithful to the source and still wrong for part of its intended audience.

A better workflow attaches eligibility conditions to the claim before translation. The German page can then use the approved local statement or omit the unsupported promise. A language reviewer should not be expected to discover product entitlement rules from prose alone.

Now add a displayed price. Replacing a dollar sign with a euro sign is not currency conversion, local pricing approval, or tax treatment. Even a correctly formatted number can communicate the wrong commercial offer.

This is a constructed example, not a report about a particular product. It shows why translation accuracy and local business accuracy need independent sign-off. Neither check can safely stand in for the other.

A local promise needs three independent checks. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The JavaScript Internationalization API's number-formatting documentation illustrates locale-sensitive currency and numeric presentation. Formatting can change separators, symbols, and displayed precision.

It does not decide the business value being formatted. A formatting function does not set a local price, apply an exchange-rate policy, or determine which taxes belong in a quoted offer.

Keep value calculation, commercial approval, and presentation separate. Test dates, percentages, units, ranges, and decimal precision as well as currency. A decimal or date ambiguity can alter an implementation instruction even when the surrounding translation is clear.

Do not rely only on screenshots. Validate the underlying structured values and the resulting visible text. A page can look plausible while its downloadable document, form confirmation, or checkout uses a different amount.

For technical content, preserve units explicitly. A translated performance claim needs the original measurement basis and conditions, not merely a localized numeral. If the source lacks that context, localization should reveal the gap rather than make the claim sound more authoritative.

Google's guidance on localized page versions explains annotations for language and regional alternatives. Language-only tags can be valid; a country code is not mandatory for every page.

The implementation should reflect actual alternatives and follow documented requirements, including reciprocal relationships where applicable. A technically correct annotation does not verify the offer or guarantee that a particular URL will appear for every user.

Google's multi-regional and multilingual guidance also recommends distinct URLs for language versions and warns about approaches that can make variations hard to discover.

This is why an SEO checklist and a product-accuracy checklist must remain separate. Correct search signals can help describe the site's structure. They cannot repair an unavailable feature, an incorrect price, or an unsupported regional claim.

Do not manufacture regional pages with only a translated heading and unchanged main content. The visible content should be useful for the audience the page claims to serve, not merely a technical entry in an alternate-language set.

W3C's guidance on declaring language in HTML describes using the language attribute for the page and marking passages in another language where appropriate.

That supports processing and accessibility. It is not identical to Google's use of visible content to determine page language, nor is it a replacement for localized-version annotations.

Keep these mechanisms distinct in review. The document language, visible language, alternative-page relationships, and commercial market can each be correct or incorrect independently.

Test navigation, form labels, validation messages, and confirmation screens, not only the article body. A reader should not encounter a translated promise followed by an unexplained language switch at the action point.

Also provide a usable way to choose another language or market where appropriate. A visitor's location does not necessarily establish their language preference or purchasing entity. Avoid trapping people in an inferred version that they cannot change.

A useful instruction identifies the audience, terminology, approved claims, immutable values, and unresolved local facts. Ask the system to flag conflicts rather than resolve them creatively.

For example, it can preserve an approved product name, translate an explanatory paragraph, and return a review note that the payment-method statement lacks a verified regional version. That is more useful than a fluent guess.

Separate language suggestions from factual edits. A reviewer should be able to see whether the model changed style, altered a number, removed a qualification, or introduced a new capability claim.

Use a glossary, but do not treat it as complete proof of quality. The same term can require different phrasing in a user interface, technical article, and legal document. Context and qualified human review still matter.

Back-translation can reveal some differences, but it is not a complete validation method. A model can translate an incorrect promise consistently in both directions. The factual source must be checked independently of linguistic consistency.

A locale release card can make the review concrete:

This is a proposed review artifact, not a requirement to expand a simple educational page into a large approval system. Apply greater scrutiny where an incorrect local promise could cause a consequential decision, and keep the process lighter where the content makes no regional commercial claim.

Choose representative page types and high-risk claims. Verify the approved local facts, visible copy, metadata, language declarations, alternative links, forms, downloadable assets, and final action destination.

Include negative cases. What happens when a capability is unavailable in the selected market? Does the page say so clearly, or does it continue to offer a misleading action? What happens when the local price has not been approved?

Test mobile layouts and text expansion. A qualification that is present but clipped, hidden, or separated from the promise may fail the reader even though a text comparison says it exists.

Record the review scope. One reviewed page does not validate an entire language site. A translation vendor's approval of wording does not establish that the checkout or campaign destination matches the offer.

The release decision should state which locales and page versions were verified, which remain held, and who owns unresolved factual questions. A batch status of translated is not a sufficient readiness state.

When a shared source changes, identify the local versions and derivative campaigns that depend on the changed claim. Do not blindly overwrite every locale with a new translation if the local product facts differ.

Classify the change. A corrected typo, a new feature entitlement, and a revised price require different review paths. Some updates can propagate mechanically; others require a local decision before release.

Keep an effective-date record so the team can explain which version a reader encountered. If an earlier page was materially incorrect, review the appropriate correction and customer communication process rather than simply replacing the file and forgetting it.

Useful measures include unresolved local facts, stale versions awaiting review, broken alternative relationships, and mismatches between the page and its action destination. These are process indicators, not promises of ranking or revenue improvement.

AI makes producing another language version easier. The durable advantage is keeping each version connected to a promise the business can actually fulfill. Fluent translation opens the conversation. Accurate local facts are what allow the company to stand behind it.

#9603. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9602. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

#9601. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9600. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9599. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9597. I Built a React Tool to Trace Where a 464 ms Click Spent Its Time

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I clicked Log in on a demo page. Chrome measured 464 ms from the click to the next paint. That was the page’s Interaction to Next Paint (INP) at the time. Okay, so the click was slow. I still needed to figure out where the time went.

So I built react-inp-blame. It lines up the browser’s interaction timings with what React committed. The login report showed 405 ms of processing. It leaned toward the click handler because only two components re-rendered.

I started it on September 12, 2026. 0.1.0 was on npm five days later and 1.0.0 came out on October 10. No runtime dependencies, MIT license. Everything I show below runs on the live demo, so you can go click the same buttons.

On most pages, INP is the latency of the longest interaction. On busier pages it drops one high outlier for every 50 interactions. Chrome’s tools and web-vitals break the interaction down into input delay, processing and presentation.

From the press until the first event handler starts

Your handler code, and in React, the render it triggers

From the end of the handlers until the next paint

Which is useful, up to a point. In a React app "processing" is your onClick plus React's render plus whatever effects ran along the way, all lumped together, and the thing you clicked is a button nested a few components deep. When you actually sit down to fix it you want something smaller and more annoying. Which component? Which handler? How many renders? Was it even React?

React DevTools can answer some of it, if you had the profiler recording at the moment the slow click happened. Usually you didn't.

The demo is a fake photo app called Framely with a sign-in page that has a few realistic mistakes baked in. Nothing leaves the page, the sign-in is simulated.

After the sign-in, a small dark badge in the bottom left corner shows the page's INP so far. It's green at 200 ms or under, amber up to 500 and red above that.

Click the badge and you get a panel of the recent slow interactions. Click a row and it opens up with the full explanation. My run for this article had 24 interactions in it, 15 key presses in the email field, 8 in the password field, and the one click.

The typing shows a different problem. Each key press in the email field re-rendered 1,004 components, 1,000 of them PostTile cards inside a FeedPreview that sits next to the form and has nothing to do with the email. The slowest key press took 232 ms and the typical one 160. The password field went the other way. Hardly anything rendered there, the time was in its own onChange handler, and the slowest press was 168 ms.

Then there's the second half of the login story, and honestly it's the part I care about most. React rendered again 274 ms after the screen had already updated, 256 components this time and most of them PhotoTile. INP doesn't count that render at all, cause it happened after the paint the click was waiting on. Whether it really belongs to the click is a harder question, I'll get to that.

Funny thing is the browser and React already know all of this between them. They just don't share.

Event Timing gives me the interaction ID and its timing. The Long Animation Frames API records the scripts in a long frame and their forced style and layout time. For the React side I listen to the same developer tools hook that React DevTools uses. After a commit, the library walks the fiber tree and counts what rendered.

Matching them up is where it got hard. The library keeps its last eight inputs and uses event timestamps to associate commits with an interaction. A render that lands after the next paint is listed as a follow-up with its own timing. The report leaves its trigger open when the timing is the only evidence.

None of this is a stable React API, so the library checks what it reads and fails closed. If react-dom is outside 17 to 19, or the fiber tree looks different from what it expects, it switches that part off, warns once, and keeps reporting, just without component names.

The demo also has an anti-pattern lab. It's eight slow interactions, each one built around one specific mistake, and a fast one as the control. I ran every scenario once on the live site, production build, and wrote down what the library said.

Every section rebuilt from scratch during render. 251 components inside SlowRender, mostly Section

Layout effects write a style, then read a size. 881 ms of forced style and layout, PriceTicker ×400

One class change restyles 30,000 cells. 773 ms updating the screen, browser work, no script

3,000 rows re-render on each key. 1,441 components inside BigList, mostly Row

Context value is a new object every render. 801 components, 800 LineItem inside OrderSummary

Input state lives above a heavy sidebar. 602 components, 600 NavItem inside Sidebar

The click handler burns 120 ms, nothing renders. The onClick handler, 120 ms

An effect sets more state after the click commits. A 401-component render 100 ms after the paint

Nothing, it's the control. No report, nothing stood out

Same nine interactions in the chart below, split by phase. Six are mostly "working", and that's the phase where a component or handler name is actually useful. Restyle storm is nearly all "updating the screen", where a React name won't help you at all.

I kept layout thrash in the lab cause it fooled me first. It looks exactly like a React problem. 400 rows, each one sets a style in a layout effect and then reads its own size back, and the browser has to redo layout 400 times inside a single commit. In the Performance panel it's one big purple and yellow block and you'd blame React for it.

Without the long-frame timing, the report would put roughly 1.1 seconds under processing. With it, I can see how much the browser spent recalculating styles and layout. Here’s what the report said.

Restyle storm goes one step further, there's basically no script in it. React renders a single component. Then one class change makes the browser restyle 30,000 cells, and that alone is 773 ms of "updating the screen" after the handler is long done (735 ms of it is the browser's own main thread work). No component name helps here. You fix it with fewer cells or CSS containment and React doesn't come into it.

Handler hog is the boring one and I like it for that. The onClick burns 120 ms, React renders nothing, and the report says so in one line. Nobody goes digging through the component tree for a render that never happened.

Cascading effect has an INP of 16 ms. Any dashboard would call that a perfect click.

Here's what's really going on. The click commits a tiny change, an effect picks it up and sets more state, and React renders again, 401 components this time, about 100 ms after the screen already updated. INP stops at the next paint, so it stops right before the expensive bit and never sees it.

I got the wording of this note wrong at first. Up to 0.25 it said people still wait for that render, which sounds right until you run it on a real app. On hyperdx, one of the two apps it was graded on, the render after a click was more than once a live tail's timer or a route change, nothing to do with the click. So from 0.26.0 the note only says INP doesn't count it and what started it can't be told. You still get the count and the time, it just doesn't pin it on a click it may not belong to.

One package, and on most apps one line in the build config. Vite:

Next.js 14.2 or later wraps the config instead:

Next.js 15.3 to 16.2 want one more export in instrumentation-client.ts. The wrapper keeps printing that line at you until the file has it, which is annoying on purpose. React Router in framework mode, Remix, TanStack Start and Astro all write their own HTML, so each gets its own short setup in the docs.

Both plugins only run in development unless you say otherwise. With the defaults a production build gets nothing from them (on Next.js 15.3 to 16.2 the extra export stays in, as an empty function).

CI covers react-dom 17.0.2 up to 19.3.0 plus React canary, Next.js 14.2.35 up to 16.3.5 plus canary, and Vite 6.4, 7.3 and 8.3. It also installs the packed tarball into fresh apps from create-vite, create-react-router, TanStack Start's CLI and create astro, then checks that a slow click there still gets blamed on the right component. That last part caught more bugs than the unit tests did.

Most teams already ship INP somewhere and I didn't want to replace that. The web-vitals attribution build keeps doing the measuring and this adds the React part on top. The lightest setup doesn't even need the runtime on the page, only the build step that keeps component names around:

You need web-vitals 5.1 or later for that. If you want the full report, the docs have the attributeINP path, sent on to Sentry or GA4.

There's also react-inp-blame/otel, still experimental. It adds the blame to the INP event an OpenTelemetry web vitals pipeline already sends, as react_inp_blame.* attributes, so you can group and filter on it in Honeycomb, Elastic, Embrace or Grafana Faro. It doesn't import anything from OpenTelemetry or a vendor SDK. Experimental just means the attribute names could still change in a minor release, cause OpenTelemetry's browser conventions have no field yet for an interaction's target or a component.

A tool for slow clicks that makes clicks slower would be a bad joke. Every report carries overheadMs, the library's own time for that interaction, so I couldn't really hide from it even if I wanted to.

The repo's numbers are 30 fresh page loads per scenario on two of the heaviest demo scenarios, a click that re-renders 801 components and a key press that re-renders 1,441:

In my own sign-in run for this article the 24 reports cost 0.1 to 3.2 ms each. The one outlier was the first key press on the page at 12 ms. Lab scenarios came in at 0.5 to 5.6 ms, one interaction each.

Size is the other cost if you turn it on in production:

react-inp-blame/auto, everything that loads with the page

The badge and panel, loaded only when shown

react-inp-blame/web-vitals, on top of /auto

35.8 KB gzip is real weight. That's why production is opt-in with a sampleRate, and why the web-vitals path with no runtime exists at all.

The demo's header says "It can be wrong". I put that there and I meant it.

Treat a component name as a lead. In a production React build, the library uses component counts because it lacks render durations. The login report hedged between the handler and the render for that reason. Forced layout attribution also depends on the browser exposing Long Animation Frames.

Before 1.0 I set a bar for myself, at least 38 right and at most 6 wrong out of 62 verdicts on apps it had never seen. 0.25.0 got graded on two real open-source apps, hyperdx and kaneo. It got 8 right, 35 wrong and 19 misleading. So no, the bar isn't met, and the 1.0.0 changelog says that in plain words. What 1.0 promises is the API and the report shape, the fields keep their meaning through 1.x. Accuracy isn't part of that promise yet.

The next round is five everyday open-source React apps, Actual, myfin, Kresus, Manage My Damn Life and Reactive Resume. The protocol freezes the test cases before anyone looks at what the library says about them. Their integrations are still being built, so no results yet. If it blames the wrong thing on your app there's an issue form just for that, and honestly those reports help more than anything else.

Quickest way is the demo at reactinpblame.com. Everything on it is slow on purpose. Click around, read what the badge blames, then open the Performance panel in DevTools and check it, the library draws its own track there next to React's.

Add the Vite plugin or the Next.js wrapper from above, restart the dev server and click the slowest thing you know about. Code, docs and known limits are on GitHub, and the package is on npm.

How I Traced a Missing Vercel AI SDK Duration Histogram

#9596. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9595. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.
