#9584. Building Red Observatory: From Basketball Statistics to a Data Platform

It started with basketball statistics. Somehow, an old MacBook Air ended up with another job.

These two things should probably have remained separate.

Instead, at some point, I decided that simply watching basketball wasn't enough. Apparently, I also needed to collect the data, store it, process it, validate it, and build an application around it.

It's an independent, fan-built sports analytics project, beginning with Olympiacos basketball and with ambitions to eventually explore other sports.

What began as an idea for a few statistics and shot charts gradually turned into something more interesting.

And, as usual with side projects, the most interesting engineering problems weren't necessarily the ones I expected.

Collect EuroLeague data, store historical games, and build an interface where I could explore player performances, shooting patterns and team statistics.

There are already plenty of websites with basketball statistics.

I wanted to understand the data myself, experiment with visualisations, and build something that combined two things I enjoy: basketball and engineering.

The first substantial historical dataset covered Olympiacos's 2023–24 EuroLeague season.

Schedules, box scores, player statistics and shooting events.

The repaired archive contains 5,889 recorded shooting events across Olympiacos and its opponents, including 4,897 field-goal attempts.

At that point, it would have been tempting to concentrate entirely on the frontend.

After all, that's the exciting part. Nobody gets particularly enthusiastic about a database table until it produces something interesting on a screen.

But I quickly learned that collecting the data was only the beginning.

An API response arriving successfully doesn't guarantee that your database represents the original information correctly.

I discovered that rather dramatically when an early version of my importer managed to confuse Bayern Munich with Barcelona.

It was my decision to generate team identifiers from the first three characters of club names.

I wrote about that particular adventure in The API Worked. My Team IDs Didn't.

The early integration combined a community-maintained Python library with direct API requests. When I inspected what had actually reached the database, I discovered that parts of the data had not been preserved correctly.

Fixing the identifiers was one problem. Making the broader ingestion process reliable was another.

The system needed to preserve consistent relationships between games, clubs, players and statistics. It needed checks for incomplete data, missing values and mismatched records.

Not a collection of scripts I could run successfully once, forget about, and spend three hours debugging the following month.

That's where the project started becoming less about a dashboard and more about data engineering.

One of my goals was to keep the project inexpensive, understandable and maintainable by one person.

The main technologies are Python, SQLite, FastAPI, React/Vite and Cloudflare.

But there's an important distinction between how I develop the application and how people access it.

The development environment uses Python collectors, a SQLite database, FastAPI and the React frontend.

The collection pipeline prepares and validates data, then exports static JSON snapshots. These snapshots are published through Cloudflare Pages, where the React frontend reads them directly.

The production website doesn't depend on a public FastAPI server handling requests for every visitor.

The system can process data, run validations, prepare releases and maintain historical archives without exposing the entire development environment to the internet.

It also means the public application can continue working with its last published dataset even if the machine responsible for collecting updates goes offline.

It's not necessarily how I would design a large commercial sports analytics platform.

But for an independently maintained side project with a limited infrastructure budget, it makes sense.

Fewer things that need to be publicly accessible.

And fewer reasons to receive an unpleasant hosting bill.

Eventually, I got to the part I'd originally wanted to build.

The historical 2023–24 dataset contains 4,897 field-goal attempts from Olympiacos and its opponents.

To explore shooting patterns, I built an SVG basketball court and began mapping shot coordinates onto it.

Until you realise that the coordinate system used by a source dataset doesn't necessarily match the coordinate system used by your visualisation.

You need to understand the origin, orientation, scale and transformations involved.

And, more importantly, you need to check whether the resulting points are actually where they should be.

Not every statistical record necessarily contains usable spatial coordinates, either. Those attempts still belong in the statistics even when they cannot be plotted on the court.

A beautifully rendered shot chart with incorrectly transformed coordinates is still wrong.

Red Observatory now includes interactive shot charts, heatmaps, box scores, player statistics, comparisons and analytical views such as Four Factors.

Those features are the visible output of the engineering work.

But they're also useful inspection tools.

When you can explore individual games and examine the underlying statistics, you have more opportunities to notice when something doesn't make sense.

The interface isn't a substitute for automated data validation.

It gives that validation a human counterpart.

Frankie is an old MacBook Air from around 2009.

It has two gigabytes of memory, a Core 2 Duo processor, and absolutely no business being involved in modern software development.

I installed Lubuntu on it and gradually gave it a collection of responsibilities involving backups, monitoring and development services.

For Red Observatory, Frankie runs scheduled collection, transformation, validation and publication jobs.

It also handles the SQLite processing that prepares data for the public snapshots.

There is something satisfying about taking hardware that would otherwise be sitting in a drawer and finding a useful role for it.

Frankie isn't powerful. Its resources are finite, its hardware is old, and I don't want the public website depending on whether a seventeen-year-old laptop is having a good day.

That's why the public application lives independently on Cloudflare Pages.

If Frankie goes offline, visitors can continue exploring the last published dataset.

New collection and publication work simply has to resume when Frankie is available again.

I wouldn't recommend this arrangement as a universal production architecture.

But for this project, it creates a useful separation between data preparation and public delivery.

And Frankie appears to have misunderstood the concept of retirement.

One thing that side projects teach you is how much work exists between "I built a feature" and "I can keep this running."

Then discovering that something perfectly reasonable on a desktop screen behaves very differently on a phone.

And then doing it all again when new data arrives.

Over time, I've been putting more effort into making these steps repeatable rather than relying on manual intervention.

New data is collected into a separate candidate database and checked before publication.

The checks cover things like fixture identities, club and player relationships, box-score completeness, score consistency and whether shooting statistics reconcile with the recorded game data.

There are also database integrity checks and safeguards against losing previously accepted fixtures.

Once the data passes validation, the pipeline prepares a snapshot, deploys a preview and checks the publication before promoting it to production.

If collection or validation fails, the last accepted dataset remains available.

That doesn't mean the system has perfect recovery from every possible deployment failure. Some interrupted releases still require manual inspection and reconciliation.

But that's an important distinction in itself.

A process being automated doesn't mean every possible failure has been solved.

I'd rather have a reliable dataset from yesterday than publish incomplete data today just because the collection script finished without raising an exception.

A feature isn't particularly useful if changing the selected season gives you statistics from one period and a shot chart from another.

The application needs to behave as one coherent system.

That's the kind of detail that becomes more important as a side project grows.

The first substantial historical archive focused on the 2023–24 EuroLeague season.

But Red Observatory now includes data from both EuroLeague and the Greek Basketball League.

That expansion is interesting because a new competition isn't necessarily just another collection of games.

Different sources can represent fixtures, teams and statistics differently.

Not every competition exposes the same level of detail, either.

For example, the spatial shot analysis currently relies on validated EuroLeague shot-location data, while Greek Basketball League analytics use verified box-score information.

I don't want the interface to imply that every dataset supports every analytical feature.

That would make the platform look more complete than the underlying information actually permits.

And it's exactly the kind of problem that becomes easier to overlook when a side project starts accumulating more features.

If all I wanted was to find out who scored the most points in an Olympiacos game, there are considerably easier ways.

I wanted to work through the entire process.

From collecting raw data, to understanding its structure, to modelling it, validating it, exposing it, and finally making it useful through an interface.

And I wanted to do all of that with a system I could actually operate myself.

I work in data engineering, but I've increasingly become interested in the architecture surrounding the data: how systems fit together, how information moves between them, how assumptions are validated, and what it takes to keep a service maintainable.

A personal project gives me the freedom to explore those questions without needing a business requirement for every experiment.

It also means I'm responsible for every questionable engineering decision.

Red Observatory isn't a finished platform.

Basketball is the starting point, and there's still plenty to improve: data coverage, additional historical seasons, mobile usability, statistical explanations and the update process.

Longer term, I'd like to explore other Olympiacos sports too, including football, volleyball and water polo.

But I'd rather expand carefully than collect more data simply because an API makes it available.

Every new competition introduces new identifiers, statistical conventions, data gaps and assumptions.

The platform needs to be able to accommodate that complexity without turning into a collection of unrelated scripts.

That's a much more interesting problem than adding another dropdown.

The biggest change in Red Observatory hasn't been a particular visualisation or feature.

It's been the way I think about the project.

At the beginning, I wanted to display basketball statistics.

Now I think about data lineage, validation, consistency, publication boundaries and the cost of keeping a system running.

It's why the data exists in the first place.

But the engineering behind it is what makes the dashboard worth using.

And that's probably the main lesson I'll take from the project so far.

Getting data onto a screen is one thing. Building a system that can keep putting trustworthy data onto that screen is another.

Red Observatory is still small, still evolving, and still very much a side project.

But it's become a surprisingly useful place to experiment with data-platform architecture.

And all because I wanted to look at some basketball statistics.

Frankie, meanwhile, has acquired another job.

Other projects and writing: ptzivras.pages.dev

Red Observatory is an independent, unofficial fan-built analytics project and is not affiliated with Olympiacos or EuroLeague.

This is exactly the kind of build story I love — the interesting part is not the dashboard, it is the decision to make the public site survive Frankie having a bad day. Keeping the last validated snapshot live while a new candidate database fails validation is a much better trade-off than most side projects make, and using the shot charts themselves as a human check on coordinate transforms is smart. A beautifully rendered chart with a flipped origin is still wrong, and automated checks alone would not have caught that.

The Bayern ID collision is a perfect example too — deriving an ID from the first three characters feels harmless until two clubs share a prefix. Did that validation failure teach you a specific check you now run on every new competition, like verifying team and player relationships before any snapshot is published? And when a shot has no usable spatial coordinates, do you drop it from the chart or flag it for review?

#9582. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

The easiest way to run Inkling 2 locally is with the Llama App, available for macOS and Windows. After you have installed it on your computer, select your preferred GGUF quant on the Hub, click the "Use this model" button and select "Llama".

With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

#9581. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9580. Unity: This scale will produce a Variant Sprite Atlas with a packed Texture that is NPOT

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at atlas-errors.petersoncool.workers.dev

In the Variant Sprite Atlas Inspector, after you set the Scale factor, Unity shows This scale will produce a Variant Sprite Atlas with a packed Texture that is NPOT (non-power of two). This may cause visual artifacts in certain compression/Texture formats. The atlas still packs, but the warning stays attached to the asset, and on the target platform sprites can show blocky edges, sampling seams, or missing mip levels that are hard to reproduce in the editor preview.

A variant atlas takes the Master atlas's packed texture and multiplies its dimensions by the variant's Scale. Power-of-two textures have widths and heights like 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, where each dimension doubles from the last. Multiplying a POT master by a Scale that is not a clean divisor produces a packed rectangle whose width or height lands between those values, which is NPOT. Many older GPUs and several compressed texture formats were designed around POT textures: mipmapping, certain block compressors, and texture wrap modes behave most predictably when the dimensions are powers of two. The warning does not mean the atlas is broken on every device; it means the packed size may not play well with the compression format or GPU your target platform uses.

The common trigger is a Scale picked for a rough size target, such as 0.75 or 0.6, without working backward from the master's actual packed dimensions. It also appears after the master atlas is repacked at a different size, which shifts what the variant rectangle becomes even though the Scale factor itself did not change. On mobile and Web targets the compressed format in use is usually what turns the NPOT risk into visible artifacts, while desktop OpenGL or Metal may tolerate the same NPOT texture without complaint, which is why the problem often first appears in a build rather than in the editor.

Open the Master atlas it derives from and read its packed texture size from Pack Preview. Multiply that width and height by the variant Scale, and check whether either result is a power of two. Open the target platform's texture compression settings and note the format assigned to these sprites. Then compare the warning state in the variant Inspector against the actual format your build uses.

A clean variant produces packed dimensions that are both POT, or runs on a format and GPU combination that explicitly supports NPOT without restrictions. A flagged variant lands on a non-POT rectangle under a compression format that prefers POT, and the warning remains in the Inspector after repack. If the master size changes between builds, recompute the product rather than trusting an earlier check, because the same Scale can be safe on one master size and NPOT on another.

Adjust the variant so the packed texture comes back to a POT rectangle, or confirm NPOT is acceptable for the target:

After the change, repack and confirm the NPOT warning has cleared from the variant Inspector, the packed texture dimensions are POT for the chosen format, and a build on the target platform renders the sprites without seams or blockiness.

The exact engine message and source location for this atlas warning are documented in the error reference.

#9579. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

Photography by Rick Holbrook; food styling by Kaitlin Wayne.
