#9555. Meet the Developer Advocate: Grigoriy Volgin on Building inDrive's Engineering Culture from the Inside Out

Byte off more tech news than you can chew, or die coding your own dreams.

Byte off more tech news than you can chew, or die coding your own dreams.

Byte off more tech news than you can chew, or die coding your own dreams.

Meet Grigoriy Volgin, a Developer Relations specialist at inDrive based in Cyprus. In this installment of our Meet the Developer Advocate series, we explore DevRel philosophy, internal community growth, and the true meaning of developer experience. Grigoriy shares how inDrive—a global mobility platform that allows passengers and drivers to negotiate fair prices directly—cultivates a thriving, 600-strong internal engineering ecosystem.

I am Grigoriy Volgin, and I work in Developer Relations at inDrive, currently based in Cyprus. My role sits precisely at the intersection of engineering, communication, developer experience, and community building.

On a day-to-day basis, I help our engineers share their knowledge and build robust internal technical communities. This involves organizing conferences and hackathons, but it also means bringing our complex engineering stories to a global audience.

Another incredibly important part of my work is focused on improving the developer experience. It is essential to understand exactly what slows engineers down so we can help create an environment where they can focus purely on meaningful work.

inDrive is a global mobility and urban services platform. Unlike traditional ride-hailing platforms, inDrive allows passengers and drivers to agree on a fair price directly. Behind this relatively simple idea is a highly complex engineering ecosystem that operates across vastly different markets, cultures, and technological environments.

What I particularly enjoy about DevRel in this context is the ability to connect people, technology, and business. I strongly believe that a solid engineering culture is built not only through writing great code, but also through consistent knowledge sharing, deep trust, and cross-team collaboration.

For me, DevRel is a fluid mix of engineering, marketing, product, and community management. I would never limit it to just one of these areas. I think a highly effective DevRel specialist must fundamentally understand what engineers do on a daily basis, what specific problems they face, and what the company as a whole wants to achieve.

You do not necessarily need to be the absolute best engineer in the room, but you absolutely must speak the same language. Furthermore, I believe that authentic DevRel starts inside the company.

It is remarkably difficult to build a strong external developer community if you do not already have an active, engaged engineering community operating internally.

For me, this discipline is not just about organizing flashy events, publishing articles, or counting page views and social media likes. It is deeply rooted in building genuine relationships with engineers, understanding their core needs, and helping them solve real-world problems. Sometimes, something as simple as organizing a small internal meetup can bring far more tangible value to the team than sponsoring a massive external conference.

When it comes to acting as a bridge between the company and the engineers, I think everything comes down to trust. Developers should always feel entirely comfortable sharing their honest feedback with you, even when it is not something the company necessarily wants to hear.

For example, when we work on improving the Developer Experience at inDrive, I try to make sure that we remain focused on the actual problems our engineers face, rather than simply following our initial top-down assumptions.

Sometimes, this process requires actively questioning our own approach or respectfully suggesting different priorities based directly on the developer feedback we have gathered.

Of course, there are always strategic business priorities, strictly limited resources, and differing opinions across management. Not every single developer request can be implemented, and that is a completely normal part of software development.

For me, the most important thing is to maintain an open conversation flowing in both directions. You need to understand the overarching business goals, but you also need to be able to effectively translate and explain why certain technical or cultural things matter deeply to the engineering team.

At inDrive, we actively work with both internal and external engineering communities. Internally, our engineering community brings together around 600 people, including backend, mobile, frontend, QA, and platform engineers, as well as engineering managers operating from several different countries.

We maintain this ecosystem through regular technical meetups, dedicated sub-communities for different engineering disciplines, an internal Techleads Club, and regular hackathons.

Externally, we share our ongoing engineering experience with the broader industry through technical articles, conference speaking engagements, and public meetups. I think consistency is one of the main reasons our community has grown so successfully. You simply cannot organize one big event and expect to have a self-sustaining, active community immediately after that. It takes time.

Another crucial factor is giving our engineers more ownership over the community itself. We constantly encourage them to suggest their own topics, organize their own specialized meetups, and share their unique experiences.

As a DevRel specialist, my job is to act as a facilitator to support these initiatives, not to manage everything myself. In fact, some of our absolute best community activities started with a simple, direct message from an engineer who just wanted to share something interesting with their colleagues.

One of the projects I am most proud of is our recent internal hackathon at inDrive. It was our biggest hackathon so far, successfully bringing together people from different countries, disparate teams, and varying professional backgrounds into a single collaborative event.

We explicitly wanted to make it more than just a standard engineering competition. We structured it so that people could work on real business problems, experiment with new technologies, and develop creative ideas that they simply would not normally have the time to explore in their daily work.

Organizing a global hackathon is quite a logistical challenge. You have to navigate different time zones, coordinate across multiple office locations, manage online participants, and take care of a massive number of small operational details.

One of the biggest lessons I took away from this experience was that the work absolutely does not end when you announce the winners. It is equally important to help the participants continue to develop their ideas after the event concludes and to actively connect them with the right stakeholders.

For me, the ultimate best result of a hackathon is when people are so inspired that they want to continue working on their projects even after the formal competition is over.

At inDrive, we generally do not build software products specifically designed for external developers to consume, so my day-to-day experience is a bit different from a traditional SaaS DevRel role. However, we do maintain extensive internal platforms and tools where the exact same DevRel principles apply.

A fantastic recent example of this is our push for internal AI adoption. We realized early on that simply giving our engineers access to new AI tools was nowhere near enough. We needed to actively help them understand exactly how to incorporate these tools into their specific daily workflows.

To achieve this, we organized hands-on workshops, launched targeted educational programs, and highly encouraged our engineers to share their own personal experiences and practical use cases with the rest of the team.

The results were excellent. Between July and October 2026, the total number of AI tool users inside the company grew by almost 40 percent. Of course, this impressive growth was the result of several overlapping initiatives, not just DevRel.

But it proved to me that providing access to a piece of technology is only the first step. You also need to invest the time to help people understand what they can actually accomplish with it in practice.

When it comes to the content our team produces, one of my favorite recent articles is How We Scaled to 530 Aurora Clusters With a 4.5-Person DBA Team by Elizaveta Maznaya, our DBA team lead at inDrive.

It is a highly engaging story about how a remarkably small team managed to double its entire database infrastructure while simultaneously reducing the number of critical incidents from around 50 down to just eight in a six-month period.

What I really appreciate about this particular article is Liza's authentic writing style. She talks completely openly about her team's mistakes, their unsuccessful technical experiments, and the specific things she would do differently today.

The piece is packed with real production numbers, deep technical details, and even some well-placed humor. I think this exact combination is why this type of content works so well. It is clearly written by an engineer, specifically for other engineers, without trying to sell them anything.

As a DevRel specialist, my primary goal is to help our engineers maintain their own unique voice when we collaborate on technical content. I would much rather publish an article with a bit of genuine personality than a perfectly polished corporate success story.

Measuring the impact of DevRel can be tricky, but we track several distinct groups of metrics at inDrive to ensure we are moving in the right direction.

One of my absolute favorite metrics to watch is the number of unique engineers involved in internal knowledge sharing. It is incredibly important for me to see new speakers and first-time authors stepping forward, rather than just working with the same five people all the time.

I also make a point to look closely at what happens long after an activity concludes. Did a promising hackathon project actually move forward into production? Did engineers genuinely start using a new internal tool after attending a workshop?

I do not ignore basic metrics like likes, impressions, or event registrations, but I absolutely do not want to optimize our daily work for these numbers alone. They are useful indicators, but they do not always tell us how much actual value we have brought to the engineers.

When we sit down to prepare a technical article or draft a conference talk, I consistently encourage our engineers to include real-world examples, actual code snippets, detailed architecture diagrams, and hard numbers wherever possible.

It is also incredibly important to talk openly about our mistakes and transparently explain exactly why certain difficult decisions were made along the way.

The exact same principle applies heavily to our internal community efforts. For example, when we organize learning sessions about new AI tools, I heavily prefer live demos where engineers show exactly how they actually use these tools in their daily work, rather than presentations about the theoretical potential of AI.

Of course, not absolutely everything needs to include code. Sometimes, simply sharing an unsuccessful experiment or breaking down a difficult engineering decision can be just as valuable. My job in DevRel is to help our engineers share their experience, not to turn it into a marketing story.

There is a well-known saying that developers are allergic to marketing. I do not entirely agree with that premise. I think developers are not allergic to marketing itself; they just naturally reject marketing that brings them no value.

When we work on technical content at inDrive, I try to keep the final product as close as possible to the engineer's original story. We help with the structure, editing, and distribution, but the technical expertise and opinions should always come from the author.

I also firmly believe that engineers are the absolute best brand ambassadors a technology company could ever ask for. A developer authentically sharing their experience at a local meetup can sometimes do more for your tech brand than an expensive marketing campaign.

Another critically important aspect is choosing the right communication channels. You need to deeply understand where your audience spends their time, what they read, and what specific problems they are interested in solving.

Kathy Sierra argues that the primary goal is to make users awesome, rather than just making the product look awesome. That idea is foundational to how I approach my work.

I see Developer Relations as a specialized way to help our engineers grow professionally. We are here to help them become confident public speakers, to guide them as they publish their first technical articles, and to support them in building their own communities.

The exact same philosophy applies to Developer Experience. It is not about promoting internal tools, but about helping engineers do their complex jobs better and with less friction.

For me, a truly great result is when someone who once needed our DevRel support eventually steps up and starts actively helping other engineers grow alongside them.

Building a thriving engineering culture requires more than just deploying new tools; it requires deep trust, authentic communication, and a relentless focus on solving real developer problems. By prioritizing internal community building and practical knowledge sharing, Grigoriy Volgin and the team at inDrive prove that the most effective Developer Relations strategies start from the inside out.

Min Kim, Founder and CEO of SODAX, on the Future of Programmable Finance

From repetitive manual tasks to a tested and customizable open-source CLI.

Automation is one of the fundamental principles of DevOps and software engineering. However, even developers who automate complex infrastructure and deployment workflows often perform repetitive tasks when starting a new software project.

Creating directories, initializing Git repositories, configuring remote repositories, and opening development environments are simple operations. When repeated frequently, however, they become unnecessary friction in the development workflow.

This observation motivated me to develop Init Flow, an open-source command-line interface written in Bash to automate and standardize project initialization.

The project combines Linux automation, Git, GitHub CLI, software engineering practices, and continuous integration into a lightweight development tool.

In this article, I will introduce Init Flow, demonstrate its capabilities, explain its architectural decisions, and share lessons learned while developing and releasing version v0.2.0.

A typical project initialization workflow might involve several manual commands:

The challenge was not simply to combine commands into a shell script, but to create a reliable, predictable, and maintainable CLI.

Init Flow automates project initialization through a single command:

The goal is to reduce repetitive work while maintaining control over the initialization process.

Init Flow is distributed under the MIT License and is currently focused on Linux environments.

Authenticate with GitHub CLI if necessary:

Clone the published version of the repository:

The installer creates a symbolic link in:

Make sure this directory is available in your PATH.

This initializes a local project, creates a public GitHub repository, and opens Visual Studio Code.

The uninstaller removes only the symbolic link associated with the expected installation.

The first release focused on establishing a functional project initialization workflow.

Version v0.2.0 — Configuration and Customization extends that foundation with seven command-line options.

These options make Init Flow adaptable to different development workflows.

The README is generated locally. Init Flow does not automatically commit or push it.

This workflow requires Git but does not require GitHub CLI authentication or Visual Studio Code.

Dry-run mode displays the planned operation without creating directories, initializing Git repositories, creating remote repositories, or opening the editor.

Remote repository availability is not verified during a dry run.

One of the main architectural goals was to keep the implementation simple without sacrificing reliability.

Rather than introducing external frameworks or additional runtime dependencies, Init Flow uses Bash and existing development tools.

The repository is organized around clear responsibilities:

The main executable handles command execution, while installation, uninstallation, testing, and documentation remain separated.

Version v0.2.0 introduces centralized argument parsing.

Arguments are validated before operations that modify the filesystem or interact with GitHub.

For example, combining --local with --private is rejected because repository visibility has no meaning when no remote repository is created.

Not every execution mode requires the same dependencies.

Checking dependencies according to the selected execution mode avoids imposing unnecessary requirements on users.

Init Flow resolves the base project directory using the following precedence:

This allows users to customize their development environment without modifying the source code.

Relative paths and paths containing spaces are also supported.

Shell automation can become dangerous when user input is passed directly to system commands without validation.

For this reason, Init Flow prioritizes defensive programming.

The implementation uses Bash strict mode:

However, strict mode alone is not sufficient. Reliable shell scripts also require explicit validation and appropriate error handling.

The project follows several defensive principles:

Dry-run mode adds another layer of operational safety by allowing users to inspect planned actions before execution.

Repository visibility remains public by default for backward compatibility. Users working with private projects should explicitly select --private or use --local.

A major goal of Init Flow is to demonstrate that even relatively small shell-based tools benefit from structured software engineering practices.

The project evolved from 30 automated tests in v0.1.0 to 58 automated tests in v0.2.0.

Integration tests use mocks to simulate external commands such as Git, GitHub CLI, and Visual Studio Code where appropriate.

This prevents automated tests from accidentally creating real GitHub repositories or interacting with external services.

ShellCheck is used to identify common shell scripting problems, including quoting issues, unsafe expansions, and other potentially unreliable patterns.

#9553. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9552. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9550. Phaser 3: Invalid Texture Atlas JSON Hash given, missing 'frames' Object

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at atlas-errors.petersoncool.workers.dev

While the atlas loads, the Console prints Invalid Texture Atlas JSON Hash given, missing 'frames' Object. The texture registers with only its base frame, and any lookup by frame name comes back empty or falls back to the first frame. Animations built from the atlas run with missing frames, sprites show the wrong tile, and the missing-frame warning follows once the animation tries to resolve names that were never parsed.

Phaser's Hash atlas parser expects a JSON object whose top level contains a frames object keyed by frame name. The parser checks for that key first; when it is absent, it aborts the parse and keeps only the __BASE frame, so every named frame later in the file is ignored. The missing key usually means one of four mismatches. The atlas was exported in Array format, a JSON whose top level holds a frames array of records, but the code feeds it through the Hash loader, or the reverse. The JSON was truncated, hand-edited, or saved as text so its structure no longer parses as the expected object. The request returned an HTML error page or a redirect body instead of the JSON file, and the parser tried to read that markup as atlas data. Or the JSON and the image were paired under mismatched keys, so the atlas that loads does not match the texture the animation references.

A re-export from the packing tool is the most common time for this to surface, because the exporter's format option can change between projects, and an old loader config kept from the previous atlas then points at the new structure. The JSON can also look almost correct at a glance: a frames entry may exist one level deeper, or the file may use the Array records while the code expects name keys.

Open the atlas JSON in a text editor and read its top-level keys. A Hash atlas exposes an object under frames, with entries keyed by frame name; an Array atlas exposes frames as a list of records that each carry a filename field. Check the browser Network panel for the JSON request and confirm the response status is 200 and the body is JSON rather than an HTML error page. Also confirm the loader call passes both the image and the JSON under matching keys.

After it loads, print the frame names the texture actually holds:

A healthy Hash atlas lists named frames such as walk_1, walk_2. A broken one lists only the base frame, or an empty list, which confirms the parser stopped before reading the frames object.

Match the exporter format to the loader you call, and repair the JSON before pairing it with the image:

After the change, verify in code rather than by watching the canvas: log frameTotal and check that each expected frame name returns true from has, and confirm the parser warning no longer appears in the Console on load.

The exact engine message and source location for this atlas warning are documented in the error reference.

#9548. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9546. BlazorJS or SpawnJS? Which to use, and how to move

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at spawndev.com

SpawnDev has two libraries that let C# use browser APIs: SpawnDev.BlazorJS and SpawnDev.SpawnJS. If you are starting a project, or you already use one, you will want to know which to pick and what moving costs.

The short answer: start new projects on SpawnJS. If your app runs well on BlazorJS, there is no rush; it is still supported. When you do move, most of your code stays the same.

SpawnDev.BlazorJS was first published in December 2022 and has over 222,000 NuGet downloads. It works through Blazor's own JavaScript interop.

SpawnDev.SpawnJS is the newer library. It talks to JavaScript through .NET's JSImport and JSExport and does not need Blazor at all.

The SpawnJS README reports a test app that went from about 30 MB to about 9 MB when trimmed. In the small example below, the published apps were 19.5 MB on SpawnJS and 22.5 MB on BlazorJS, counting the compressed copies of each file.

Because SpawnJS does not depend on Blazor, the same C# can run where Blazor never does: a plain .NET WebAssembly app, a Web Worker, a browser extension, or a .NET WebAssembly console app running under Node.js with no browser at all.

That last one is not a curiosity. SpawnDev.ILGPU, our GPU library, runs its shared GPU test suite that way: a .NET WebAssembly console app under Node.js, using SpawnJS for every JavaScript call, with real WebGPU from the webgpu npm package, the Dawn project's own binding. On an RTX 4070, all 876 tests that apply there pass. The other 22 are skipped: 17 belong to other backends, and 5 check for a feature Node does not have, such as a canvas or a video frame, and say so.

The first run found something a browser-only test run never could: under Node, the library never loaded one of its WebGPU helper scripts, so dispatch batching quietly switched off. That is fixed in SpawnDev.ILGPU 5.4.52.

To try it yourself, Example 08 runs a GPU kernel from C# under Node and prints the GPU it found. It needs Node 22 or later and the .NET wasm-tools workload.

BlazorJS is built on Blazor's own interop, so it needs a Blazor app.

Article 1 built a recipe page that keeps the screen awake and copies to the clipboard with SpawnJS. We wrote the same page with BlazorJS, and the same browser tests pass for both.

The page itself did not change except for one line, the runtime you inject:

Everything else, Navigator, WakeLock, Clipboard, the += and -= events, using, is the same in both libraries.

2. Change the start-up lines in Program.cs.

3. Change the namespaces in _Imports.razor and your C# files: SpawnDev.BlazorJS becomes SpawnDev.SpawnJS, and SpawnDev.BlazorJS.JSObjects becomes SpawnDev.SpawnJS.JSObjects.

4. Change the injected runtime: BlazorJSRuntime becomes SpawnJSRuntime.

Your own wrappers. If you wrote classes for a JavaScript library, the base class and the reference type change: JSObject becomes SpawnJSObject, and the constructor takes a SpawnJSObjectReference instead of an IJSInProcessObjectReference. Both libraries' own Audio wrapper shows it:

Calls by name. BlazorJS takes the arguments as objects and names only the return type. SpawnJS names every argument type, then the return type:

The compiler points at each of these, so the move is a list of build errors to work through, not a hunt.

Matching packages. Several libraries come in both families, such as SpawnDev.BlazorJS.WebWorkers and SpawnDev.SpawnJS.WebWorkers, and SpawnDev.BlazorJS.Cryptography and SpawnDev.SpawnJS.Cryptography. Move each to its SpawnJS twin at the same time.

Both versions of the page are in the example repo:

The SpawnJS version is in BrowserApis, next to it.

#9545. Your Coding Agent Shouldn't Be Able to Close Its Own Ticket, Part 2: What the Comments Changed

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at arbituro.com

What's a claim worth if the code has moved on since it was made?

That's not my question. It came from the comments on part one, and it was a better question than anything I'd asked in the post itself. 🙌

Quick recap if you missed it. Part one argued that a coding agent should be able to claim a ticket is done, with evidence, but never decide it. A CI check or a named person decides. The agent keeps all its speed; it just doesn't mark its own work.

The comments agreed with the split, and then politely took it apart at the edges. This post is about those edges, and what got built because of them.

Two commenters shaped this post, so they go first.

Glenn left three comments, and each one turned into a change. The first: tie every completion claim to the exact commit it was made against, or the approval ends up attached to stale evidence. The last: the same permission boundary should cover the checks, because an agent that can edit the CI config can weaken the very thing that judges it.

Gautam K put the principle more sharply than I did: the ticket can only close when something the agent can't edit confirms it. The agent can propose Done. Only that check, or a person, can move it.

Thank you both. Most of what's below exists because you wrote it down. 🙇

Here's the scenario Glenn described. The agent claims a criterion is met:

(OK, a better agent writes what it actually checked. Stay with me.)

Then it keeps going. It pushes a refactor. Then a "small fix". By the time a person reads the claim, it's about code that no longer exists. The evidence was real. It's just evidence about a different commit. 😬

So now every claim is pinned to a commit. When a coding agent claims a criterion, Arbituro records the commit the job's branch or pull request stood at right then.

The important part: the agent doesn't send that commit. Arbituro reads it from the job's link, which only GitHub's own events move. An agent can't leave it out, and it can't name a convenient one. A commit the agent reports would just be more testimony. A commit GitHub reports is a fact. 🔒

When more code lands after the claim, the person deciding sees it right next to the claim, in plain words: "2 commits pushed since". After a force push it says "The branch was rewritten since the claim" instead.

And opening the claim shows what GitHub recorded after it, oldest first: each check that reported and the commit it ran on, each commit pushed with its subject and the first files it touched, and the merge. You don't have to go and dig through GitHub to find out what "2 commits" means.

This was the real design question, and I went back and forth on it.

Withdrawing the claim automatically sounds safer. But agents push constantly, and plenty of pushes don't touch what was claimed. A fix to a typo in the README shouldn't throw away a claim about checkout. Auto-withdrawing would mean the person deciding never sees most claims at all.

So a moved head warns and never withdraws. The claim stays there to decide. The person can still press Met, or press "Ask it to check again", which leaves a note on the job for the agent, under their own name. The agent reads it the next time it opens the job:

Short, specific, and it names the commit. No "please re-verify everything". 🎯

One more honesty detail I care about: the wording always says "since the claim", never "since the agent checked". Arbituro knows where the branch stood when the claim arrived. It doesn't know exactly what the agent looked at. The screen shouldn't pretend it does. 🧐

The same logic applies to CI, and this one is stricter.

A check's pass is only true of the commit it ran on. So when a new commit lands on the pull request, any criterion a named check had already passed goes back to undecided until that check reports again on the new commit.

No warning this time, a reset. Why the difference? A person's judgement might survive a small push; they can look and decide. A check's pass is a statement about one exact commit, and nothing else. What happened (the job's history) records which criterion was reopened, by which check, and both commits.

Claims can also carry screenshots now, for anything a screen proves. "Works on mobile" with an actual phone-sized screenshot beats "works on mobile" with a ✅. 📱

Glenn's last comment is the one I keep thinking about.

Taking "close the ticket" away from the agent doesn't help much if the same pull request can quietly change what "passing" means. Edit the workflow so the test job skips the slow suite. Loosen CODEOWNERS. The check goes green, the criterion ticks, and everything looks verified. ✅ 🙃

Agents running inside Arbituro can't write under .github at all. That covers workflows, the actions they call, and CODEOWNERS. It's enforced in code, on the files about to be pushed, not in a prompt. And a person still approves the change after that.

A coding agent in your own repo is different. Claude Code, Cursor and friends work in your checkout with your permissions. Arbituro can't stop them editing a workflow, and it shouldn't pretend to. That's what branch protection, required reviews and CODEOWNERS are for.

What Arbituro can do is make sure a weakened check never passes quietly. So before a named check ticks a criterion, Arbituro reads the pull request's changed files from GitHub. If any of them are under .github/, or a CODEOWNERS file, the criterion still ticks, but its line says so, in warning colour. Roughly:

The path links straight to the pull request's changed files on GitHub. The person signing the job off sees it at exactly the moment it matters.

All of that made the evidence better. But look at what the person deciding still had in front of them: the agent's own account of its own work, plus a pile of GitHub facts to cross-check by hand.

I got bitten by exactly this on my own backlog. A coding agent claimed the suite passed. Two minutes later, the Frontend check failed on the very commit it had claimed. The only place that said so was a log I wasn't looking at. 🤦

The facts were all there. Nobody had put them next to the claim.

So now every claim gets read by a second agent before its person decides. Think of it as a verification agent:

Here's how that looks on a job's Done when. (A sample job, but the real screen.) The coding agent claimed three criteria at the same commit, and the reader went through all three:

The verdict leads each claim, so you can see which one needs you before reading anything. When a claim holds up, the reader's reason is one quiet line. When it doesn't, you get the whole reason.

And the bottom row is Problem Three doing its job: the check passed, on a pull request that also touched the CI workflow.

Open the claim that doesn't hold up, and everything is in one place: the agent's word, what GitHub recorded after it, and the reading.

The agent said the suite passed. GitHub says the check failed on that exact commit. The reader put the two side by side, so I didn't have to. And it caught the second problem too: "tests pass" isn't evidence that a postcode gets refused. 🎯

Is an agent checking an agent just turtles all the way down? 🐢 A bit. But this reader can't edit the claim, can't edit GitHub's record, and can't tick anything. Its only power is to put the contradiction in front of the person who decides. That's a power I'm happy to hand out.

Part one said: whoever wrote the change doesn't approve it.

This round added three things, and they're all versions of the same idea:

The first two weren't on my list before the comments. That's the best argument I know for writing in public. 😄

Arbituro is free for up to three people at arbituro.com.

How do you keep the checks independent of the agent being checked? Code owners on CI, checks that run from outside the repo, or mostly trust and a careful eye on the diff?

And if you think warn-not-withdraw is the wrong call for a stale claim, I want to hear that one too. Part three might be yours. 👇

#9544. Not Mayo Or Butter: Grilled Cheese Is Even Tastier With One Creamy Store-Bought Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A classic grilled cheese is a thing of both beauty and comfort. And of course, a simple sandwich such as this is open to interpretation, with many putting their own spin on it, like making it Swiss-style with raclette cheese or switching up the grilling process by using an air fryer, like Ree Drummond. But there's an easy addition you can make to your next grilled cheese that will make it even tastier (and it's not mayo or butter, though you can certainly use either): It's store-bought caramelized onion dip.

When spread onto the bread and covered in cheese, then warmed through in a hot pan, caramelized onion dip brings a burst of flavor and a compelling texture to the sandwich. Of course, it's definitely savory, but the caramelized onions also introduce a subtly sweet element to grilled cheese, creating a flavor sensation that is much more interesting for your taste buds. Meanwhile, the dip melts into the cheese, adding to the creaminess, while the onions introduce a little toothsome variety to chew on, beyond the softness of the filling and the crispness of the bread.

Trader Joe's Caramelized Onion Dip is one great store-bought option, and it's part of the store's regular lineup, so you should be able to find it year-round (unless it has sold out). Whole Foods also sells a version under its 365 brand, which Amazon Prime members can shop for on Amazon.

If you have the desire to take things a step further, you might try a mix-in or two that can elevate the taste of the dip (and therefore, your entire sandwich). That might include some dried cranberries, which can help draw out the aforementioned sweetness of the onions, creating an even bolder contrast in your salty grilled cheese. You also might play to the richness and crumble up some crisp bacon into the base. Or enhance the savory, aromatic vibes by adding both thinly sliced scallions and chives.

Now, if you're having trouble finding caramelized onion dip at your grocery store, you could always make your own, though cooking down the onions properly can be laborious. If standing over your stove for 45 minutes doesn't appeal to you, Ina Garten cuts down on the time by using a larger pot, which allows the onions to cook more evenly and efficiently. But if you'd rather skip the cooking altogether, you might find the adjacent caramelized onion jam on store shelves. This won't be as creamy as the dip, but it will still impart that same rich, savory, and slightly sweet flavor, so it's a decent substitution.

#9543. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9540. Catching "Nest can't resolve dependencies" without running the app

I'm a Salesforce developer, and I build IDE plugins on the side. When I went looking for a framework to build my first public one for, NestJS stood out for one reason: its most common error is completely predictable from the source code, but you only find out about it when the app starts.

Here's what I learned about why it happens, and how you can check for it without running anything.

OrdersModule imports UsersModule, so it looks like it should work. It doesn't, because importing a module only gives you what that module exports. UsersModule provides UsersService but never exports it.

Inside a module, a class can inject something if:

That's the whole rule. Everything else is detail.

Because the rule is that simple, you can check it by reading files:

The useful part is that you also know how to fix it, because you can see where the class is provided. If UsersService is provided in UsersModule but not exported, the fix is "export it from UsersModule". If it's already exported, the fix is "import UsersModule into OrdersModule". If nobody provides it, the fix is "add it to providers".

A checker that is wrong even occasionally gets switched off, so most of the work went into deciding what not to report:

The rule is to only report a missing provider when every module that could supply it is visible in the source.

The same module graph gives you circular import detection almost for free. Run a strongly connected components pass (Tarjan's algorithm) over the imports graph. Any component with more than one module is a cycle. Then a breadth-first search inside that component gives you the shortest loop to show the user, like UsersModule → AuthModule → UsersModule, instead of a list of every module involved.

I turned this into a plugin for WebStorm and IntelliJ called Nest Assist. The free version gives you a route list, go-to-handler by URL and a module graph. The paid version runs checks like the one above in the editor, with quick fixes.

I don't use Nest day to day, so I'm sure real projects have setups I haven't thought of. If you know a wiring pattern that would trip up a check like this, I'd really like to hear about it in the comments.

#9538. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9536. Add This Creamy Ingredient To Ground Beef For A Juicier Burger With Extra Protein

Incorporating secret ingredients into your burger patties elevates the dish in unexpected ways. Some components flavor the meat while others enhance the texture. For an add-in that does both — with a delicious underlying creaminess — look no further than yogurt. The dairy works as a ground beef tenderizer, making a burger that's softer and full of moisture. Not to mention, yogurt is an effective enhancement in chicken or turkey patties, too.

Yogurt's contained lactic acid functions as a mild, but nevertheless efficient, tenderizer, lightly marinating the meat. The inclusion of a liquid naturally adds lots of moisture to a burger — you certainly won't have to worry about a disappointingly dry result. Plus, the ingredient lends the burger a lightly creamy mouthfeel.

And if you use Greek yogurt for the task, you'll get a nice dose of added protein, too. Mix in a quarter cup of whole milk Greek yogurt — a quantity suitable for a pound of meat — and you'll up the dish by 5.5 grams of protein. This yogurt's extra fat content will further prevent dryness, all while forming a patty that's not too loose, making a burger rendition that stands out.

Working yogurt into your beef patties doesn't require any special technique. You can simply stir the dairy with the beef in a bowl, seasoning with salt and pepper in parallel. Follow by forming the patties as usual, then lightly brush the exterior with oil to prevent unwanted adhesion. Prepare the yogurt burgers using your preferred method, whether you're fond of using a skillet or grilling burgers like a pro. However, if you notice your mixture appears too wet, consider adding a binder — chia seeds are a fantastic option to absorb moisture but keep things tender and juicy; panko breadcrumbs will also absorb excess liquid while keeping the bite of each burger soft.

Such a burger tastes delicious with classic seasonings, but don't rule out creative modifications, too. The pairing of yogurt and beef recalls Greek and Middle Eastern cuisine, so consider integrating Eastern Mediterranean seasonings into the build.

A Greek burger spin could fold in oregano, lemon, and feta — core flavors of a Greek salad. A kofta-style patty might up the spice, working in earthy cumin, a dash of spicy harissa, and grated garlic into the mix. Alternatively, season the meat in a sweet direction by using simply turmeric and onions; the ingredients will set you up for a wide array of flavorful condiments. Build out the meal with an aromatic herbal yogurt sauce, a bold dose of roasted peppers, or a marinated arugula salad, and you'll make a burger rendition that'll become a frequent part of the rotation.

#9535. Give Canned Baked Beans A Delicious Upgrade With A Drizzle Of This Ingredient (Hint: It's Not Honey)

When you need a side to go along with your main dinner entree and you need one fast, it's reassuring to know that shelf-stable, pantry-sitting canned goods have got your back. Included in Food Republic's list of inexpensive canned foods you'll use all the time are beans, and along with the plain black or red varieties (which typically need to be combined with other ingredients to make a reasonable side), you could also reach for scrumptious, creamy baked beans. But while they're totally fine heated up straight from the can, they can certainly benefit from a drizzle of molasses.

Molasses might not be the first thing you think of when you consider add-ins, but many homemade recipes call for it, and for good reason. Made by boiling down sugarcane juice or refining sugar, the rich, thick syrup is slightly smoky and sweet, with robust, burnt caramel notes, making it a perfect match for deepening the flavor of sometimes weak-tasting canned baked beans and bringing them closer to homemade.

It is for this reason that molasses is also preferable to honey here. Honey is intensely sweet, can taste almost floral at times, and has a delicate flavor, whereas molasses is bolder and has a meatier taste that can make its presence known among the other ingredients in the dish.

It's important to note that there are three main types of molasses: light, dark, and blackstrap, and they each have different flavor profiles. For canned baked beans, you'll likely want to stick with light or dark because blackstrap is intensely bitter (also, light is the sweetest of the three, so if sweetness is important to you, go with that one). If you're heating the beans on the stove, you can start by drizzling in about half a tablespoon of molasses per 28-ounce can, bringing the mixture to a boil, and then simmering for about 10 minutes. If you're baking them, likewise, just stir in the molasses before putting the dish in the oven — it couldn't be simpler.

If you don't have any molasses sitting about, don't panic. There are plenty of other additions that can help upgrade canned baked beans and make them taste less, well, pantry-fied. Take brown sugar, for example — did you know that it's often just white sugar and molasses combined? A little bit will still bring that sweet contrast to balance out the savory flavors and give you a deeper, more complex finish.

Another great option is one you might normally use on your pancakes: maple syrup. You don't want to use the fake stuff that's primarily made of corn syrup and artificial flavors and colors, but rather 100% real Grade A maple syrup for the best flavor. Its sweetness again deliciously contrasts with and enhances the canned baked beans' savoriness, while the maple flavor adds its unique caramelly, toffee-like notes to the dish.

#9533. Make Your Next Breakfast Sandwich Korean-Style For A Major Fiber & Flavor Boost

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Think of Korean cuisine, and a sandwich likely isn't the first thing that comes to mind. However, bread-based dishes are widely enjoyed in the East Asian country, both in cafes and as street food. An especially popular breakfast rendition is gilgeori toast, a comforting breakfast sandwich stuffed with eggs and shredded vegetables.

Easy-to-make, packed with fiber, and delicious, the dish is a great candidate for your breakfast rotation. Traditionally, this sandwich calls for a fluffy loaf of milk or brioche bread, the buttery soft texture turning crisp on the outside once toasted. Meanwhile, the filling comprises a variable shredded vegetable medley: Cabbage traditionally forms the centerpiece, joined by carrots, onions, scallions, and often garlic chives. Mixed with egg and then pan-fried into an aesthetic golden-brown patty, the filling delectably complements the soft bread. Gilgeori is usually rounded out with a sprinkle of sugar and a drizzle of ketchup and mustard.

It's an assembly that easily comes together during bleary morning hours, yet nevertheless offers a nutritious start to the day. One sandwich can pack in around six ounces of shredded cabbage, which amounts to over 4 grams of fiber. Add up the fiber from a tablespoon of carrot, two of sliced onion, and two whole green onions, and you're including another 1.5 grams. Then, add in two slices of thick-cut brioche sandwich bread, and you've got an extra 2. That's about 7.5 grams, which is around a quarter of what you need a day, already knocked out by breakfast. Mixed with the roughly 6.5 grams of protein from the egg alongside filling bread, the sandwich serves as a terrific way to start the day.

The morning isn't always the best time to precisely reconstruct a recipe. Thankfully, gilgeori toast welcomes a wide array of reinterpretations and ingredients. Starting with the bread, feel free to swap the milk bread for sourdough, whole wheat, or even a convenient store-bought whole grain like Ezekiel or Dave's Killer. You'll lose out on some of the dish's airiness, but potentially gain extra fiber content in the process. Two slices of Dave's Killer 21 Whole Grains and Seeds contain some 8 grams of fiber, more than doubling the total of the sandwich.

Up the satiation further by adding on a slice of seared ham, a filling also enjoyed in Korea. And cheese is always welcome, whether American, cheddar, or fontina – Martha Stewart's go-to for breakfast sandwiches. Instead of the sugar sprinkle, lend the dish a sweet note by using jam: Raspberry or cherry jam makes a great fit. Not to mention, you can replace the ketchup and mustard with a condiment of your preference; you can buy a bottle of Gochujang Sriracha Hot Sauce online, for instance. The template of bread and shredded vegetables works with many flavors, perfect for morning enjoyment.

#9532. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9531. Not Cinnamon: Add A Pinch Of This Warm Spice To French Toast For A Flavor Boost

Warm spices on French toast create a cozy, aromatic breakfast dish that warms your sinuses as much as your tongue. While traditional cinnamon is always a solid choice, cardamom French toast adds new layers of fresh, almost herbal notes for something far more complex and just as compatible with your other favorite seasonings.

Some folks call cardamom the queen of spices — and for good reason. As flavorful as it is versatile, it's a shelf-stable ingredient that lasts a long time, grinds easily into a powder, and seems to taste amazing with just about any sweet recipe you could think of. While it can be a tad on the expensive side, small amounts suffuse your French toast with deep flavor, so even a small jar of seeds can last you quite a while. The key is to mix it with your other dried spices to create a delicate flavor profile similar to mulled drinks, festive winter desserts, and spiced ciders.

Six pods should yield about half a teaspoon of ground spice, enough for roughly six pieces of French toast (though pod sizes vary). Since you want a smooth batter without much texture, it's best to grind the seeds into a fine powder before mixing. The moisture from eggs and milk should help protect the delicate spice, but remember that heat affects the flavor release of spices. Gently toasting the pods beforehand is a great way to bump up the flavor without using more of the pricey ingredient.

Though cardamom has quite a bit of flavor, it's also rather delicate and can slip into the background or be the star of the show, depending on your preferences. In sweet dishes, there are few warm spices it pairs poorly with, and more obscure ingredients can really elevate its flavor for something showstopping.

Just about any warming spice you'd associate with the colder months should pair beautifully with cardamom. Cinnamon is a bold counterpart that can carry most of the flavor profile without overshadowing it when used in moderation. Allspice and cloves are a match made in heaven, providing an almost berry-like warmth to counteract cardamom's cool, herbal notes. Ground or fresh ginger can add a touch of sharpness that offers quite a bit of contrast, providing a similar bite on the tongue to garlic that's far more compatible with sugary bases.

If you really want to bump up the flavor of cardamom, don't stick to just spices. Floral notes from things like dried and ground orange peels, lychee, or guava really round out your French toast without overpowering your spices. These are highly compatible with cardamom and make your breakfast taste almost like a pomander, with an incredible bouquet of aromas the second your bread hits the pan. You can also use food-safe flavoring oils instead, mixing them into your wet ingredients for greater control over how much flavor you're adding.
